::: {.lm-hero}
[Chapter 7 · Regularization]{.eyebrow}

# Ridge and LASSO

[A single penalty term trades a little bias for a large drop in variance; the shape of that penalty decides whether coefficients merely shrink or vanish outright.]{.dek}
:::

A model with enough parameters can pass through every training point and still predict
badly, because it has fit the noise along with the signal. [Regularization]{.term} adds a
penalty on the size of the coefficients to the training loss, so the fit has to pay for
complexity it cannot justify. The penalty buys a small increase in bias in exchange for a
large reduction in variance.

::: {.defbox}
[Regularized Cost]{.lbl}
[ J(&theta;) = Loss(data, &theta;) + &lambda; &middot; Penalty(&theta;) ]{.math}
:::

The knob $\lambda$ sets the strength. Two penalties dominate practice and differ in one
respect that changes everything. [Ridge]{.term} squares the coefficients, $\sum_j \theta_j^2$,
and has a closed form. [LASSO]{.term} takes their absolute values, $\sum_j |\theta_j|$, has
no closed form, and can set coefficients to *exactly* zero. This page builds both from the
linear algebra up, watches their coefficient paths diverge, and shows the geometry that
explains why only one of them selects features.

## The overfitting it cures

Fifteen noisy points come from $y = \sin(2\pi x)$. A degree-9 polynomial has enough freedom
to chase every wiggle, and ordinary least squares takes the bait: its coefficients blow up to
hundreds of thousands. Ridge solves the same normal equation with $m\lambda I$ added to the
cross-product, leaving the intercept unpenalized. That one term tames the fit.

::: {.defbox}
[Ridge Estimate]{.lbl}
[ &theta;&#770;<sub>ridge</sub> = (X<sup>&#8868;</sup>X + m&lambda;I)<sup>&#8722;1</sup> X<sup>&#8868;</sup>y ]{.math}
:::

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Fifteen fixed points from y = sin(2*pi*x) + noise
x = np.array([0.3745, 0.9507, 0.732, 0.5987, 0.156, 0.156, 0.0581, 0.8662,
              0.6011, 0.7081, 0.0206, 0.9699, 0.8324, 0.2123, 0.1818])
y = np.array([0.5377, -0.582, -1.7774, -0.2958, 1.0756, 0.3734, 0.2285, -0.9679,
              -0.8044, -1.6074, -0.0599, -0.0086, -0.101, 1.0904, 0.9463])

def poly(x, d):                       # design matrix [1, x, x^2, ..., x^d]
    return np.column_stack([x**k for k in range(d + 1)])

def ridge(X, y, lam):
    m, n = X.shape
    P = lam * m * np.eye(n); P[0, 0] = 0.0  # do not penalize the intercept
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + P, X.T @ y)

degree = 9
X = poly(x, degree)
theta_ols   = ridge(X, y, 0.0)             # lambda = 0 is plain OLS
theta_ridge = ridge(X, y, 1e-2)
print(f"max|theta|  OLS  : {np.abs(theta_ols).max():12.1f}")
print(f"max|theta|  ridge: {np.abs(theta_ridge).max():12.1f}")

grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
G = poly(grid, degree)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.scatter(x, y, s=70, color="#076FA1", edgecolor="white", zorder=5, label="training data")
ax.plot(grid, np.sin(2*np.pi*grid), color="#666666", lw=2, ls="--", label="true function")
ax.plot(grid, G @ theta_ols,   color="#2FC1D3", lw=2.2, label="degree-9 OLS (overfit)")
ax.plot(grid, G @ theta_ridge, color="#31417A", lw=2.2, label="ridge (lambda=0.01)")
ax.set_ylim(-2, 2); ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e3da", lw=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## R
```{webr}
# Fifteen fixed points from y = sin(2*pi*x) + noise
x <- c(0.3745, 0.9507, 0.732, 0.5987, 0.156, 0.156, 0.0581, 0.8662,
       0.6011, 0.7081, 0.0206, 0.9699, 0.8324, 0.2123, 0.1818)
y <- c(0.5377, -0.582, -1.7774, -0.2958, 1.0756, 0.3734, 0.2285, -0.9679,
       -0.8044, -1.6074, -0.0599, -0.0086, -0.101, 1.0904, 0.9463)

poly_features <- function(x, d) outer(x, 0:d, `^`)   # [1, x, x^2, ..., x^d]

ridge_fit <- function(X, y, lambda) {
  n <- ncol(X); m <- nrow(X)
  P <- lambda * m * diag(n); P[1, 1] <- 0            # do not penalize the intercept
  solve(t(X) %*% X + P, t(X) %*% y)
}

degree <- 9
X <- poly_features(x, degree)
theta_ols   <- ridge_fit(X, y, 0)                    # lambda = 0 is plain OLS
theta_ridge <- ridge_fit(X, y, 1e-2)
cat(sprintf("max|theta|  OLS  : %12.1f\n", max(abs(theta_ols))))
cat(sprintf("max|theta|  ridge: %12.1f\n", max(abs(theta_ridge))))

grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 200)
G <- poly_features(grid, degree)
plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "#076FA1", cex = 1.4, ylim = c(-2, 2), xlab = "x", ylab = "y", bty = "l")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)
lines(grid, sin(2*pi*grid),       col = "#666666", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(grid, G %*% theta_ols,      col = "#2FC1D3", lwd = 2.2)
lines(grid, G %*% theta_ridge,    col = "#31417A", lwd = 2.2)
legend("topright", c("training data", "true function", "degree-9 OLS", "ridge (0.01)"),
       col = c("#076FA1", "#666666", "#2FC1D3", "#31417A"),
       pch = c(19, NA, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, 2, 1, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

:::

Ridge cuts the largest coefficient from roughly $3 \times 10^5$ down to about $1.4$. The two
languages agree to that figure, but their OLS maxima differ in the fifth significant digit
(about 318026 versus 318018). That gap is not a bug; it is the symptom. The unpenalized
cross-product is so close to singular that two linear solvers round it differently. Adding
$m\lambda I$ removes the pathology, and both report the same $1.4$.

## What adding $m\lambda I$ does

The ridge estimate changes one thing about least squares: before inverting
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$, it adds $m\lambda$ to each diagonal entry. The figure below follows
that change through the book's example of floor area against number of rooms (Section 7.2),
with twelve houses at about 25 square meters per room. On standardized features,
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ stretches the direction in which both coefficients rise together far
more than the direction that trades one against the other. Equation 7.2 of the book writes the
ridge solution in exactly these two directions, with the stretches as $d_j^2$.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/lm-ix.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById('ix-ridge'), L = window.LMIX, $ = s => root.querySelector(s);
  // Twelve houses at about 25 m² per room, generated at 4 thousand € per m² and nothing per room
  // (tools/ch07_ridge_houses.py, seed 1971). The book's Section 7.2 example, given numbers.
  const AREA  = [117, 81, 144, 117, 146, 74, 155, 99, 148, 75, 86, 148];
  const ROOMS = [5, 3, 6, 5, 6, 3, 6, 4, 6, 3, 3, 6];
  const PRICE = [459, 339, 565, 388, 579, 309, 647, 390, 590, 304, 358, 627];
  const m = AREA.length, mean = a => a.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0) / a.length;
  const sd = a => { const u = mean(a); return Math.sqrt(mean(a.map(v => (v - u) ** 2))); };
  const SA = sd(AREA), SR = sd(ROOMS);
  const Z1 = AREA.map(v => (v - mean(AREA)) / SA), Z2 = ROOMS.map(v => (v - mean(ROOMS)) / SR);
  const YC = PRICE.map(v => v - mean(PRICE));
  const dot = (a, b) => a.reduce((s, v, i) => s + v * b[i], 0);
  const G = [[dot(Z1, Z1), dot(Z1, Z2)], [dot(Z1, Z2), dot(Z2, Z2)]];   // X^T X, standardized
  const XTY = [dot(Z1, YC), dot(Z2, YC)];
  // The two directions of X^T X and their stretches (eigenvalues, the book's d_j^2)
  const tr = G[0][0] + G[1][1], det = G[0][0] * G[1][1] - G[0][1] ** 2, rad = Math.sqrt(tr * tr / 4 - det);
  const unit = v => { const n = Math.hypot(v[0], v[1]); return [v[0] / n, v[1] / n]; };
  const S1 = tr / 2 + rad, S2 = tr / 2 - rad;
  const V1 = unit([G[0][1], S1 - G[0][0]]);                                // both up
  let V2 = unit([-V1[1], V1[0]]); if (V2[0] < 0) V2 = [-V2[0], -V2[1]];    // area up, rooms down
  const E1 = V1[0] * XTY[0] + V1[1] * XTY[1], E2 = V2[0] * XTY[0] + V2[1] * XTY[1];   // the data's evidence
  const comps = lam => [E1 / (S1 + m * lam), E2 / (S2 + m * lam)];
  const solve = lam => { const k = comps(lam); return [k[0] * V1[0] + k[1] * V2[0], k[0] * V1[1] + k[1] * V2[1]]; };
  const mse = t => mean(YC.map((y, i) => (y - t[0] * Z1[i] - t[1] * Z2[i]) ** 2));
  const OLS = solve(0), MSE0 = mse(OLS), K0 = comps(0), KMAX = Math.max(Math.abs(K0[0]), Math.abs(K0[1]));
  let lam = 0;

  const f3 = v => Math.abs(v) >= 100 ? v.toFixed(0) : Math.abs(v) >= 10 ? v.toFixed(1) : Math.abs(v) >= 1 ? v.toFixed(2) : v.toFixed(3);
  const big = v => Math.abs(v) < 100 ? v.toFixed(1) : Math.round(v).toLocaleString('en-US');
  const sf = v => v < 1 ? v.toFixed(3) : v.toFixed(2);              // stretches: 23.85, 0.148
  function matrix(ml) {
    const cell = (v, add) => add ? `<td>${f3(v)} <span class="add">+ ${f3(add)}</span></td>` : `<td>${L.fmt(v, 2)}</td>`;
    $('.m-fwd').innerHTML = `<span class="lhs">X<sup>⊤</sup>X + mλI =</span><table><tr>${cell(G[0][0], ml)}${cell(G[0][1])}</tr><tr>${cell(G[1][0])}${cell(G[1][1], ml)}</tr></table>`;
  }
  function steps(C, ml) {
    const k = comps(lam), S = [S1, S2], E = [E1, E2], col = [C.blue, C.orange];
    const bar = (j, frac) => `<div class="bar" style="color:${col[j]};width:${Math.max(0.3, 100 * Math.min(1, Math.abs(frac)))}%"></div>`;
    const div = j => '÷ ' + (ml > 0 ? `(${sf(S[j])} <span style="color:${C.orange}">+ ${f3(ml)}</span>)` : sf(S[j]));
    let h = `<div></div><div class="h" style="color:${C.blue}">both up</div><div class="h" style="color:${C.orange}">area against rooms</div>`;
    h += `<div class="lab">The data's evidence along each direction (X<sup>⊤</sup>y)</div>` +
         [0, 1].map(j => `<div><div class="num">${big(E[j])}</div>${bar(j, E[j] / E1)}</div>`).join('');
    h += `<div class="lab">divided by the stretch, <i>d</i>² + <i>m</i>λ</div>` +
         [0, 1].map(j => `<div><div class="num wrap">${div(j)}</div></div>`).join('');
    h += `<div class="rule"></div><div class="lab">= the coefficient's component</div>` +
         [0, 1].map(j => `<div><div class="num">${f3(k[j])}</div>${bar(j, k[j] / KMAX)}</div>`).join('');
    h += `<div class="lab">kept, against least squares</div>` +
         [0, 1].map(j => `<div><div class="num">${pct(S[j] / (S[j] + ml))}</div>${bar(j, S[j] / (S[j] + ml))}</div>`).join('');
    $('.ix-steps').innerHTML = h;
  }
  const pct = v => v === 1 ? '100%' : 100 * v >= 99.5 ? '>99%' : 100 * v < 1 ? '<1%' : (100 * v).toFixed(0) + '%';

  const P = { x0: 56, x1: 548, y0: 12, y1: 310, X: [-45, 292], Y: [-124, 80] };   // 1.46 px per unit on both axes
  const px = v => P.x0 + (v - P.X[0]) / (P.X[1] - P.X[0]) * (P.x1 - P.x0);
  const py = v => P.y1 - (v - P.Y[0]) / (P.Y[1] - P.Y[0]) * (P.y1 - P.y0);
  const PATH = [OLS].concat(Array.from({ length: 140 }, (_, i) => solve(10 ** (-4 + i * 6.5 / 139))));
  function coef(C, t, k) {
    const svg = $('.ix-coef'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    L.el('rect', { x: P.x0, y: P.y0, width: P.x1 - P.x0, height: P.y1 - P.y0 }, L.el('clipPath', { id: 'ixr-clip' }, svg));
    const g = L.el('g', { 'clip-path': 'url(#ixr-clip)' }, svg);
    [0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250].forEach(v => L.el('line', { x1: px(v), x2: px(v), y1: P.y0, y2: P.y1, stroke: C.grid }, g));
    [-100, -50, 0, 50].forEach(v => L.el('line', { x1: P.x0, x2: P.x1, y1: py(v), y2: py(v), stroke: C.grid }, g));
    L.contours((a, b) => mse([a, b]), P.X, P.Y, [120, 1200, 6000].map(d => MSE0 + d), 120)
      .forEach((cl, j) => cl.segs.forEach(s => L.el('line', { x1: px(s[0]), y1: py(s[1]), x2: px(s[2]), y2: py(s[3]), stroke: j === 0 ? C.cyan : C.axis, 'stroke-width': j === 0 ? 1.5 : 1 }, g)));
    L.el('polyline', { points: PATH.map(p => px(p[0]) + ',' + py(p[1])).join(' '), fill: 'none', stroke: C.fs, 'stroke-width': 1.3, 'stroke-dasharray': '5 4', opacity: 0.55 }, g);
    if (lam > 0) {
      L.contours((a, b) => mse([a, b]), P.X, P.Y, [mse(t)], 160)
        .forEach(cl => cl.segs.forEach(s => L.el('line', { x1: px(s[0]), y1: py(s[1]), x2: px(s[2]), y2: py(s[3]), stroke: C.fs, 'stroke-width': 1.5 }, g)));
      L.el('circle', { cx: px(0), cy: py(0), r: Math.hypot(t[0], t[1]) * (P.x1 - P.x0) / (P.X[1] - P.X[0]), fill: 'none', stroke: C.muted, 'stroke-width': 1.3, 'stroke-dasharray': '6 5' }, g);
    }
    // the solution as the sum of its components: along "both up", then along "area against rooms"
    const a = [k[0] * V1[0], k[0] * V1[1]];
    L.arrow(g, [px(0), py(0)], [px(a[0]), py(a[1])], C.blue, 3);
    if (Math.hypot(k[1] * V2[0], k[1] * V2[1]) > 4) L.arrow(g, [px(a[0]), py(a[1])], [px(t[0]), py(t[1])], C.orange, 3);
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(OLS[0]), cy: py(OLS[1]), r: 6, fill: '#fff', stroke: C.fs, 'stroke-width': 2.2 }, g);
    L.el('text', { x: px(OLS[0]) - 10, y: py(OLS[1]) - 8, 'text-anchor': 'end', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.fs }, g).textContent = 'least squares';
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(t[0]), cy: py(t[1]), r: 6.5, fill: C.fs, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 1.5 }, g);
    if (lam > 0) L.el('text', { x: px(t[0]) + 11, y: py(t[1]) + 5, 'font-size': 15, fill: C.fs }, g).textContent = 'ridge';
    L.el('line', { x1: P.x0, x2: P.x1, y1: P.y1, y2: P.y1, stroke: C.axis }, svg);
    L.el('line', { x1: P.x0, x2: P.x0, y1: P.y0, y2: P.y1, stroke: C.axis }, svg);
    [0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250].forEach(v => L.el('text', { x: px(v), y: P.y1 + 19, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v);
    [-100, -50, 0, 50].forEach(v => L.el('text', { x: P.x0 - 7, y: py(v) + 5, 'text-anchor': 'end', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v);
    L.el('text', { x: (P.x0 + P.x1) / 2, y: 356, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = 'area coefficient (standardized)';
    L.el('text', { x: 13, y: (P.y0 + P.y1) / 2, transform: `rotate(-90 13 ${(P.y0 + P.y1) / 2})`, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = 'rooms coefficient (standardized)';
  }

  function note(t, k) {
    const ml = m * lam, per = [t[0] / SA, t[1] / SR];
    if (lam === 0) return 'Least squares. The data offer little evidence along area against rooms, ' + big(E2) + ' against ' + big(E1) + ', but the matrix stretches that direction only ' + sf(S2) + ', so the division makes it the larger component, ' + f3(k[1]) + '. That component is what turns houses generated at 4 per m² and nothing per room into ' + L.fmt(per[0]) + ' per m² and ' + L.fmt(per[1], 1) + ' per room.';
    if (ml < 0.5 * S2) return 'mλ = ' + f3(ml) + ' is still small next to the stretch of ' + sf(S2) + ', so the division barely changes: the area-against-rooms component is ' + f3(k[1]) + '.';
    if (ml <= 2 * S2) return 'mλ = ' + f3(ml) + ' is about the size of the small stretch, ' + sf(S2) + ', so it roughly doubles the divisor and halves the area-against-rooms component, to ' + f3(k[1]) + '. Next to ' + sf(S1) + ', the same mλ leaves “both up” at ' + f3(k[0]) + '.';
    const room = per[1] > 0 ? ' The price per room is now positive: shrinking one component moved a single coefficient away from zero.' : '';
    if (ml <= S1 / 19) return 'mλ = ' + f3(ml) + ' dominates the small stretch and barely touches the large one. The component the data barely support falls to ' + f3(k[1]) + '; the one they pin down stays at ' + f3(k[0]) + '.' + room;
    if (ml <= S1) return 'mλ = ' + f3(ml) + ' dominates the small stretch and now shrinks the large one too, though far less. The component the data barely support keeps ' + pct(S2 / (S2 + ml)) + ' of its least-squares size, at ' + f3(k[1]) + '; the one they pin down keeps ' + pct(S1 / (S1 + ml)) + ', at ' + f3(k[0]) + '.' + room;
    return 'mλ = ' + f3(ml) + ' is now large against both stretches, so both components shrink and the solution heads toward zero.';
  }

  function update() {
    const C = L.colors(root), ml = m * lam, t = solve(lam), k = comps(lam);
    matrix(ml); steps(C, ml); coef(C, t, k);
    L.stat($('.t-c'), 0, false, () => L.fmt(t[0] / SA) + ' · ' + L.fmt(t[1] / SR, 1));
    L.stat($('.t-k'), (S1 + ml) / (S2 + ml), false, v => L.fmt(v, 1));
    $('.ix-note').textContent = note(t, k);
  }

  const showLam = v => v <= -3.995 ? '0' : (10 ** v) >= 1 ? (10 ** v).toFixed(1) : (10 ** v).toPrecision(2);
  const sl = L.slider($('.ix-l'), $('.ix-lv'), showLam, v => { lam = v <= -3.995 ? 0 : 10 ** v; update(); });
  L.presets($('.ix-buttons'), [
    { label: 'Least squares (λ = 0)', action: () => sl.set(-4) },
    { label: 'mλ = small stretch', action: () => sl.set(Math.log10(S2 / m)) },
    { label: 'λ = 0.1', action: () => sl.set(-1) },
    { label: 'λ = 1', action: () => sl.set(0) },
  ]);
  sl.refresh();
})();
</script>
</div>
```


## Two penalties, two paths

A [coefficient path]{.term} plots each coefficient as $\lambda$ sweeps from small to large.
Ridge has its closed form; LASSO needs an iterative solver. The standard one is
[coordinate descent]{.term}: cycle through the coefficients, and update each to minimize the
cost with the others held fixed. For the L1 penalty that one-dimensional minimum has a tidy
form, [soft-thresholding]{.term}, which shrinks a coefficient toward zero and clips it to
exactly zero once the penalty outweighs its correlation with the residual.

::: {.defbox}
[Soft-Thresholding (one LASSO coordinate)]{.lbl}
[ &theta;<sub>j</sub> = sign(&rho;<sub>j</sub>) &middot; max(|&rho;<sub>j</sub>| &minus; m&lambda;/2, 0) / &Sigma;<sub>i</sub> x<sub>ij</sub>&sup2; ]{.math}
:::

Here $\rho_j$ is the dot product of feature $j$ with the residual formed by leaving feature
$j$ out. We standardize the polynomial features first, so a single $\lambda$ penalizes every
coefficient on equal footing. The two panels tell the whole story: ridge coefficients glide
toward zero but never arrive, while LASSO coefficients hit zero one after another. At
$\lambda = 0.05$ ridge keeps all eight features and LASSO keeps two.

Coordinate descent alone crawls on features as correlated as these powers of $x$: at the
smallest $\lambda$ values it needs hundreds of thousands of sweeps. The cells add two
accelerations. They fit from the strongest penalty to the weakest, starting each fit from the
previous solution, and every ten sweeps they take the current nonzero coefficients and their
signs as a guess, solve the optimality conditions on that set exactly, and stop once the
result passes them. (`glmnet` in R and `Lasso` in scikit-learn are the production solvers.)

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.array([0.3745, 0.9507, 0.732, 0.5987, 0.156, 0.156, 0.0581, 0.8662,
              0.6011, 0.7081, 0.0206, 0.9699, 0.8324, 0.2123, 0.1818])
y = np.array([0.5377, -0.582, -1.7774, -0.2958, 1.0756, 0.3734, 0.2285, -0.9679,
              -0.8044, -1.6074, -0.0599, -0.0086, -0.101, 1.0904, 0.9463])

def poly(x, d):
    return np.column_stack([x**k for k in range(d + 1)])

def ridge(X, y, lam):
    m, n = X.shape; P = lam * m * np.eye(n); P[0, 0] = 0.0
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + P, X.T @ y)

def polish(X, y, t, theta, tol):
    # Take the nonzero set and signs from theta, solve the optimality equations
    # on that set exactly, and repair the guess: zero a coefficient whose sign
    # flips, admit a zero one whose gradient exceeds t. None if that fails.
    n = X.shape[1]
    s = np.sign(theta); s[0] = 1.0                    # intercept always in
    for _ in range(2 * n):
        S = np.flatnonzero(s)
        cand = np.zeros(n)
        cand[S] = np.linalg.solve(X[:, S].T @ X[:, S],
                                  X[:, S].T @ y - t * s[S] * (S > 0))
        flip = (S > 0) & (np.sign(cand[S]) != s[S])
        if flip.any():
            s[S[flip]] = 0.0; continue
        g = X.T @ (y - X @ cand)
        viol = np.where(s == 0, np.abs(g) - t, -np.inf)
        if viol.max() <= tol:
            return cand
        j = int(np.argmax(viol)); s[j] = np.sign(g[j])
    return None

def lasso(X, y, lam, theta=None, max_sweeps=10000, tol=1e-10):
    m, n = X.shape
    t = lam * m / 2
    theta = np.zeros(n) if theta is None else theta.copy()   # warm start
    col_sq = (X**2).sum(axis=0)
    for sweep in range(1, max_sweeps + 1):
        for j in range(n):
            r = y - X @ theta + X[:, j] * theta[j]   # residual without feature j
            rho = X[:, j] @ r
            if j == 0:                                # intercept: no penalty
                theta[j] = rho / col_sq[j]
            else:                                     # soft-threshold
                theta[j] = np.sign(rho) * max(abs(rho) - t, 0.0) / col_sq[j]
        if sweep % 10 == 0:
            exact = polish(X, y, t, theta, tol)
            if exact is not None:
                return exact, sweep
    raise RuntimeError(f"no convergence at lambda={lam}")

# Standardize the polynomial columns (not the intercept) so lambda is comparable
degree = 8
X = poly(x, degree)
mu = X[:, 1:].mean(axis=0); sd = X[:, 1:].std(axis=0)
Xs = X.copy(); Xs[:, 1:] = (X[:, 1:] - mu) / sd

lams = np.logspace(-4, 1, 40)
ridge_path = np.array([ridge(Xs, y, l)[1:] for l in lams])
lasso_path, theta, sweeps = [], None, []
for l in lams[::-1]:                                  # strong to weak, warm starts
    theta, k = lasso(Xs, y, l, theta)
    lasso_path.append(theta[1:]); sweeps.append(k)
lasso_path = np.array(lasso_path[::-1])
print(f"LASSO: most sweeps at any lambda = {max(sweeps)} (cap 10000)")

lam0 = 0.05
nz_r = int(np.sum(np.abs(ridge(Xs, y, lam0)[1:]) > 1e-6))
nz_l = int(np.sum(np.abs(lasso(Xs, y, lam0)[0][1:]) > 1e-6))
print(f"at lambda={lam0}: ridge keeps {nz_r}/{degree} coefs, LASSO keeps {nz_l}/{degree}")

# Cycle the book-blue family so each coefficient keeps one color across panels
path_colors = ["#076FA1", "#31417A", "#2FC1D3", "#666666"]   # BLUE, FS_BLUE, CYAN, GRAY
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), sharey=True)
for j in range(ridge_path.shape[1]):
    c = path_colors[j % len(path_colors)]
    axes[0].plot(lams, ridge_path[:, j], lw=1.6, color=c)
    axes[1].plot(lams, lasso_path[:, j], lw=1.6, color=c)
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["Ridge: shrink, never zero", "LASSO: snap to zero"]):
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.axhline(0, color="#666666", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_xlabel("lambda"); ax.set_title(t, loc="left")
    for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e3da", lw=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## R
```{webr}
x <- c(0.3745, 0.9507, 0.732, 0.5987, 0.156, 0.156, 0.0581, 0.8662,
       0.6011, 0.7081, 0.0206, 0.9699, 0.8324, 0.2123, 0.1818)
y <- c(0.5377, -0.582, -1.7774, -0.2958, 1.0756, 0.3734, 0.2285, -0.9679,
       -0.8044, -1.6074, -0.0599, -0.0086, -0.101, 1.0904, 0.9463)

poly_features <- function(x, d) outer(x, 0:d, `^`)

ridge_fit <- function(X, y, lambda) {
  n <- ncol(X); m <- nrow(X); P <- lambda * m * diag(n); P[1, 1] <- 0
  solve(t(X) %*% X + P, t(X) %*% y)
}

polish <- function(X, y, t, theta, tol) {
  # Take the nonzero set and signs from theta, solve the optimality equations
  # on that set exactly, and repair the guess: zero a coefficient whose sign
  # flips, admit a zero one whose gradient exceeds t. NULL if that fails.
  n <- ncol(X)
  s <- sign(theta); s[1] <- 1                       # intercept always in
  for (it in seq_len(2 * n)) {
    S <- which(s != 0)
    cand <- rep(0, n)
    XS <- X[, S, drop = FALSE]
    cand[S] <- solve(t(XS) %*% XS, t(XS) %*% y - t * s[S] * (S > 1))
    flip <- (S > 1) & (sign(cand[S]) != s[S])
    if (any(flip)) { s[S[flip]] <- 0; next }
    g <- drop(t(X) %*% (y - X %*% cand))
    viol <- ifelse(s == 0, abs(g) - t, -Inf)
    if (max(viol) <= tol) return(cand)
    j <- which.max(viol); s[j] <- sign(g[j])
  }
  NULL
}

lasso_fit <- function(X, y, lambda, theta = NULL, max_sweeps = 10000, tol = 1e-10) {
  m <- nrow(X); n <- ncol(X); t <- lambda * m / 2
  if (is.null(theta)) theta <- rep(0, n)            # else warm start
  col_sq <- colSums(X^2)
  for (sweep in seq_len(max_sweeps)) {
    for (j in seq_len(n)) {
      r   <- y - X %*% theta + X[, j] * theta[j]    # residual without feature j
      rho <- sum(X[, j] * r)
      if (j == 1) {                                 # intercept: no penalty
        theta[j] <- rho / col_sq[j]
      } else {                                      # soft-threshold
        theta[j] <- sign(rho) * max(abs(rho) - t, 0) / col_sq[j]
      }
    }
    if (sweep %% 10 == 0) {
      exact <- polish(X, y, t, theta, tol)
      if (!is.null(exact)) return(list(theta = exact, sweeps = sweep))
    }
  }
  stop(sprintf("no convergence at lambda=%g", lambda))
}

# Standardize the polynomial columns (not the intercept) so lambda is comparable
degree <- 8
X <- poly_features(x, degree)
sds <- apply(X[, -1], 2, function(c) sqrt(mean((c - mean(c))^2)))   # population sd
Xs <- X; Xs[, -1] <- scale(X[, -1], center = colMeans(X[, -1]), scale = sds)

lams <- 10^seq(-4, 1, length.out = 40)
ridge_path <- t(sapply(lams, function(l) ridge_fit(Xs, y, l)[-1]))
lasso_path <- matrix(0, length(lams), degree); theta <- NULL; sweeps <- 0
for (i in rev(seq_along(lams))) {                   # strong to weak, warm starts
  fit <- lasso_fit(Xs, y, lams[i], theta)
  theta <- fit$theta; lasso_path[i, ] <- theta[-1]; sweeps <- max(sweeps, fit$sweeps)
}
cat(sprintf("LASSO: most sweeps at any lambda = %d (cap 10000)\n", sweeps))

lam0 <- 0.05
nz_r <- sum(abs(ridge_fit(Xs, y, lam0)[-1]) > 1e-6)
nz_l <- sum(abs(lasso_fit(Xs, y, lam0)$theta[-1]) > 1e-6)
cat(sprintf("at lambda=%.2f: ridge keeps %d/%d coefs, LASSO keeps %d/%d\n",
            lam0, nz_r, degree, nz_l, degree))

# Cycle the book-blue family so each coefficient keeps one color across panels
path_colors <- c("#076FA1", "#31417A", "#2FC1D3", "#666666")   # BLUE, FS_BLUE, CYAN, GRAY
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(lams, ridge_path, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 1.6, col = path_colors, log = "x", bty = "l",
        xlab = "lambda", ylab = "coefficient", main = "Ridge: shrink, never zero")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)
abline(h = 0, col = "#666666", lty = 2)
matplot(lams, lasso_path, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 1.6, col = path_colors, log = "x", bty = "l",
        xlab = "lambda", ylab = "coefficient", main = "LASSO: snap to zero")
grid(col = "#e6e3da", lty = 1, lwd = 0.6)
abline(h = 0, col = "#666666", lty = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

:::

## Why only LASSO selects

The contrast is geometric. Minimizing the loss subject to a budget on the coefficients is the
same as the penalized form, and the budget draws a constraint region. The cells below draw
both regions for two coefficients and find each solution by searching the region's boundary.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Polygon

ols = np.array([1.0, 2.2])                      # the least-squares solution
def loss(t1, t2):                               # training error, up to a constant
    return 0.35 * (t1 - ols[0])**2 + (t2 - ols[1])**2

r = 1.3                                         # the budget on the coefficients
# Least squares lies outside both regions, so each solution lies on the region's
# boundary: walk the boundary and keep the point with the lowest loss.
a = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 20001)
circle = np.column_stack([r * np.cos(a), r * np.sin(a)])
t = np.linspace(-r, r, 10001)
diamond = np.vstack([np.column_stack([t, r - np.abs(t)]),
                     np.column_stack([t, np.abs(t) - r])])
ridge = circle[np.argmin(loss(circle[:, 0], circle[:, 1]))]
lasso = diamond[np.argmin(loss(diamond[:, 0], diamond[:, 1]))]
print(f"ridge: theta = ({ridge[0]:.2f}, {ridge[1]:.2f})")
print(f"LASSO: theta = ({lasso[0]:.2f}, {lasso[1]:.2f})")

T1, T2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 300), np.linspace(-2, 3.8, 300))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5.0))
panels = [(axes[0], "Ridge: a circle", ridge, Circle((0, 0), r), "#076FA1"),
          (axes[1], "LASSO: a diamond", lasso,
           Polygon([(r, 0), (0, r), (-r, 0), (0, -r)]), "#2FC1D3")]
for ax, title, sol, shape, col in panels:
    ax.contour(T1, T2, loss(T1, T2), levels=[0.25, 2, 4, 7, 11],
               colors="#cfccc2", linewidths=0.8)
    ax.contour(T1, T2, loss(T1, T2), levels=[loss(*sol)],   # the contour through the solution
               colors="#31417A", linewidths=1.6)
    shape.set(fill=False, edgecolor=col, linewidth=2.5)
    ax.add_patch(shape)
    ax.axhline(0, color="#666666", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="#666666", lw=0.8)
    ax.scatter(*ols, marker="*", s=200, color="#31417A", zorder=5, label="least squares")
    ax.scatter(*sol, s=110, color=col, edgecolor="white", zorder=6, label="solution")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(-2, 3.8)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_1$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\theta_2$")
    ax.text(0.03, 0.97, title, transform=ax.transAxes, va="top", fontsize=11,
            bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=2))
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left")
    for s in ["top", "right"]:
        ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## R
```{webr}
ols <- c(1.0, 2.2)                                # the least-squares solution
loss <- function(t1, t2) 0.35 * (t1 - ols[1])^2 + (t2 - ols[2])^2

r <- 1.3                                          # the budget on the coefficients
# Least squares lies outside both regions, so each solution lies on the region's
# boundary: walk the boundary and keep the point with the lowest loss.
a <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 20001)
circle <- cbind(r * cos(a), r * sin(a))
t <- seq(-r, r, length.out = 10001)
diamond <- rbind(cbind(t, r - abs(t)), cbind(t, abs(t) - r))
ridge <- circle[which.min(loss(circle[, 1], circle[, 2])), ]
lasso <- diamond[which.min(loss(diamond[, 1], diamond[, 2])), ]
cat(sprintf("ridge: theta = (%.2f, %.2f)\n", ridge[1], ridge[2]))
cat(sprintf("LASSO: theta = (%.2f, %.2f)\n", lasso[1], lasso[2]))

g1 <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 300); g2 <- seq(-2, 3.8, length.out = 300)
L <- outer(g1, g2, loss)
draw_panel <- function(title, sol, col, shape) {
  contour(g1, g2, L, levels = c(0.25, 2, 4, 7, 11), col = "#cfccc2", drawlabels = FALSE,
          asp = 1, bty = "l", xlab = expression(theta[1]), ylab = expression(theta[2]))
  contour(g1, g2, L, levels = loss(sol[1], sol[2]), col = "#31417A", lwd = 1.6,
          drawlabels = FALSE, add = TRUE)            # the contour through the solution
  abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "#666666")
  if (shape == "circle") lines(r * cos(a), r * sin(a), col = col, lwd = 2.5)
  else polygon(c(r, 0, -r, 0), c(0, r, 0, -r), border = col, lwd = 2.5)
  points(ols[1], ols[2], pch = 8, col = "#31417A", cex = 1.6)
  points(sol[1], sol[2], pch = 19, col = col, cex = 1.6)
  title(title, adj = 0, line = 0.6, font.main = 1)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
draw_panel("Ridge: a circle", ridge, "#076FA1", "circle")
draw_panel("LASSO: a diamond", lasso, "#2FC1D3", "diamond")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

:::

The star is the least-squares solution, and each gray ellipse joins coefficient pairs with
equal training error, the error growing from one ellipse to the next away from the star. The
solution sits where the smallest ellipse that still reaches the region touches its boundary:
the dark one. Ridge's region is a circle, smooth everywhere, so the contact point lands almost
anywhere; here it is $(0.32, 1.26)$, with both coefficients nonzero. LASSO's region is a
diamond, and its corners sit on the axes. An ellipse sliding in from outside tends to strike a
corner first, here at $(0, 1.30)$, and a corner means one coefficient is exactly zero. That is
feature selection falling out of the shape of the penalty.

The plot above fixes one budget. The figure below lets it grow, with the same loss and the
same least-squares point: a circle and a diamond of size $t$, and the share of the budget each
method gives $\theta_1$.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/lm-ix.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  const root = document.getElementById('ix-corners'), L = window.LMIX, $ = s => root.querySelector(s);
  // The loss of the cells above: 0.35 (t1 - 1)^2 + (t2 - 2.2)^2, least squares at (1, 2.2).
  const A = [0.35, 1], C0 = [1.0, 2.2];
  const loss = (a, b) => A[0] * (a - C0[0]) ** 2 + A[1] * (b - C0[1]) ** 2;
  const OLS2 = Math.hypot(C0[0], C0[1]), OLS1 = Math.abs(C0[0]) + Math.abs(C0[1]);
  function ridge(t) {                     // min loss s.t. |theta|_2 <= t: theta_i = a_i c_i / (a_i + mu)
    if (OLS2 <= t) return C0.slice();
    const at = mu => C0.map((c, i) => A[i] * c / (A[i] + mu));
    let lo = 0, hi = 1e6;
    for (let k = 0; k < 200; k++) { const mid = (lo + hi) / 2; Math.hypot(...at(mid)) > t ? lo = mid : hi = mid; }
    return at((lo + hi) / 2);
  }
  function lasso(t) {                     // min loss s.t. |t1| + |t2| <= t; both c > 0, so the top-right edge
    if (OLS1 <= t) return C0.slice();
    let t1 = (A[0] * C0[0] + A[1] * (t - C0[1])) / (A[0] + A[1]);   // best point on t1 + t2 = t
    t1 = Math.min(Math.max(t1, 0), t);                               // a corner when it would leave the edge
    return [t1, t - t1];
  }
  let t = 1.3;

  const P = { x0: 40, x1: 385, y0: 12, y1: 357, X: [-1.4, 3.2], Y: [-1.4, 3.2] };   // equal units
  const px = v => P.x0 + (v - P.X[0]) / (P.X[1] - P.X[0]) * (P.x1 - P.x0);
  const py = v => P.y1 - (v - P.Y[0]) / (P.Y[1] - P.Y[0]) * (P.y1 - P.y0);
  function plane(C, r, l) {
    const svg = $('.ix-plane'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    L.el('rect', { x: P.x0, y: P.y0, width: P.x1 - P.x0, height: P.y1 - P.y0 }, L.el('clipPath', { id: 'ixc-clipP' }, svg));
    const g = L.el('g', { 'clip-path': 'url(#ixc-clipP)' }, svg);
    [-1, 0, 1, 2, 3].forEach(v => {
      L.el('line', { x1: px(v), x2: px(v), y1: P.y0, y2: P.y1, stroke: v === 0 ? C.axis : C.grid }, g);
      L.el('line', { x1: P.x0, x2: P.x1, y1: py(v), y2: py(v), stroke: v === 0 ? C.axis : C.grid }, g);
    });
    L.contours(loss, P.X, P.Y, [0.25, 1, 2.5, 5, 9], 90)
      .forEach(cl => cl.segs.forEach(s => L.el('line', { x1: px(s[0]), y1: py(s[1]), x2: px(s[2]), y2: py(s[3]), stroke: C.axis, 'stroke-width': 1 }, g)));
    [[r, C.blue], [l, C.cyan]].forEach(([sol, col]) => {
      if (loss(...sol) > 1e-9) L.contours(loss, P.X, P.Y, [loss(...sol)], 140)
        .forEach(cl => cl.segs.forEach(s => L.el('line', { x1: px(s[0]), y1: py(s[1]), x2: px(s[2]), y2: py(s[3]), stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 1.4, 'stroke-dasharray': '5 3' }, g)));
    });
    const k = (P.x1 - P.x0) / (P.X[1] - P.X[0]);
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(0), cy: py(0), r: t * k, fill: 'none', stroke: C.blue, 'stroke-width': 2.4 }, g);
    L.el('polygon', { points: [[t, 0], [0, t], [-t, 0], [0, -t]].map(q => px(q[0]) + ',' + py(q[1])).join(' '), fill: 'none', stroke: C.cyan, 'stroke-width': 2.4 }, g);
    L.el('text', { x: px(C0[0]) + 10, y: py(C0[1]) - 8, 'font-size': 14, fill: C.fs }, g).textContent = 'least squares';
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(C0[0]), cy: py(C0[1]), r: 5.5, fill: C.fs }, g);
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(r[0]), cy: py(r[1]), r: 7, fill: C.blue, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 1.6 }, g);
    L.el('circle', { cx: px(l[0]), cy: py(l[1]), r: 7, fill: C.cyan, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 1.6 }, g);
    [-1, 0, 1, 2, 3].forEach(v => {
      L.el('text', { x: px(v), y: P.y1 + 18, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v;
      L.el('text', { x: P.x0 - 7, y: py(v) + 5, 'text-anchor': 'end', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v;
    });
    L.el('text', { x: (P.x0 + P.x1) / 2, y: 396, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = 'θ₁';
    L.el('text', { x: 12, y: py(2.5) + 5, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = 'θ₂';
  }
  const Q = { x0: 52, x1: 385, y0: 16, y1: 350, T: [0, 3.4], V: [-0.05, 1.05] };
  const qx = v => Q.x0 + (v - Q.T[0]) / (Q.T[1] - Q.T[0]) * (Q.x1 - Q.x0);
  const qy = v => Q.y1 - (v - Q.V[0]) / (Q.V[1] - Q.V[0]) * (Q.y1 - Q.y0);
  const TS = Array.from({ length: 241 }, (_, i) => 3.4 * i / 240);
  function path(C) {
    const svg = $('.ix-path'); svg.innerHTML = '';
    [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1].forEach(v => {
      L.el('line', { x1: Q.x0, x2: Q.x1, y1: qy(v), y2: qy(v), stroke: v === 0 ? C.axis : C.grid }, svg);
      L.el('text', { x: Q.x0 - 7, y: qy(v) + 5, 'text-anchor': 'end', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v;
    });
    [0, 1, 2, 3].forEach(v => L.el('text', { x: qx(v), y: Q.y1 + 18, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 14, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = v);
    L.el('line', { x1: Q.x0, x2: Q.x0, y1: Q.y0, y2: Q.y1, stroke: C.axis }, svg);
    [[ridge, C.blue, 'ridge'], [lasso, C.cyan, 'LASSO']].forEach(([fn, col, name], k) => {
      L.el('polyline', { points: TS.map(s => qx(s) + ',' + qy(fn(s)[0])).join(' '), fill: 'none', stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 2.6 }, svg);
      L.el('circle', { cx: qx(t), cy: qy(fn(t)[0]), r: 6, fill: col, stroke: '#fff', 'stroke-width': 1.5 }, svg);
      L.el('line', { x1: Q.x0 + 12, x2: Q.x0 + 34, y1: Q.y0 + 14 + 20 * k, y2: Q.y0 + 14 + 20 * k, stroke: col, 'stroke-width': 2.6 }, svg);
      L.el('text', { x: Q.x0 + 40, y: Q.y0 + 19 + 20 * k, 'font-size': 14, fill: C.ink }, svg).textContent = name;
    });
    L.el('line', { x1: qx(t), x2: qx(t), y1: Q.y0, y2: Q.y1, stroke: C.muted, 'stroke-dasharray': '3 4' }, svg);
    L.el('text', { x: (Q.x0 + Q.x1) / 2, y: 396, 'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 15, fill: C.muted }, svg).textContent = 'budget t';
  }
  const pair = p => '(' + L.fmt(p[0]) + ', ' + L.fmt(p[1]) + ')';
  function note(r, l) {
    if (t >= OLS1) return 'The budget no longer binds either method: both return least squares, (1.00, 2.20).';
    if (t >= OLS2 && l[0] > 0) return 'The circle no longer binds: ridge returns least squares, θ₁ = 1.00. The diamond still does, and θ₁ has entered the LASSO model at ' + L.fmt(l[0]) + ', short of its least-squares value.';
    if (l[0] === 0) return 'LASSO spends the whole budget on θ₂ and leaves θ₁ at exactly zero: the error contour first reaches the diamond at its top corner. Ridge, with the same budget, gives θ₁ ' + L.fmt(r[0]) + '. Every bit of θ₁ costs LASSO the same rate, all the way down to zero; ridge charges almost nothing for the first bit.';
    return 'The budget now reaches past the corner, so the contour first meets the diamond along its edge, and θ₁ enters the LASSO model at ' + L.fmt(l[0]) + '. Ridge has given θ₁ a share all along: ' + L.fmt(r[0]) + '.';
  }
  function update() {
    const C = L.colors(root), r = ridge(t), l = lasso(t);
    plane(C, r, l); path(C);
    L.stat($('.t-r'), 0, false, () => pair(r));
    L.stat($('.t-l'), 0, l[0] === 0, () => pair(l));
    $('.ix-note').textContent = note(r, l);
  }
  const sl = L.slider($('.ix-t'), $('.ix-tv'), v => L.fmt(v), v => { t = v; update(); });
  L.presets($('.ix-buttons'), [
    { label: 't = 1.3 (the plot above)', action: () => sl.set(1.3) },
    { label: 't = 2.5', action: () => sl.set(2.5) },
  ]);
  sl.refresh();
})();
</script>
</div>
```

## Scale your features first

The penalty couples to the scale of each feature. A coefficient on a tiny-scale feature has
to be large to matter, and a large coefficient is exactly what the penalty punishes, so an
informative variable measured in small units gets crushed while a coarse-scale variable
slides through. The fix is to standardize every feature to zero mean and unit variance before
fitting. Here the true model leans on a small-scale feature; raw, ridge nearly zeros its
coefficient, and after standardization the two stand on equal terms.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
import numpy as np

# Two features on wildly different scales; the small one carries the signal
x1 = np.array([0.011, -0.004, 0.009, -0.013, 0.006, -0.008, 0.015, -0.002,
               0.010, -0.011, 0.003, -0.007, 0.012, -0.005, 0.001])
x2 = np.array([820., -540., 410., -930., 360., -610., 1180., -150.,
               770., -880., 240., -470., 990., -330., 80.])
y  = 100*x1 + 0.001*x2 + np.array([0.02, -0.01, 0.015, -0.02, 0.01, -0.012, 0.018,
               -0.003, 0.014, -0.016, 0.005, -0.009, 0.017, -0.006, 0.002])

def ridge(X, y, lam):
    m, n = X.shape; P = lam * m * np.eye(n); P[0, 0] = 0.0
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + P, X.T @ y)

def standardize(X):
    Z = X.copy()
    Z[:, 1:] = (X[:, 1:] - X[:, 1:].mean(axis=0)) / X[:, 1:].std(axis=0)
    return Z

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x1)), x1, x2])
t_raw = ridge(X, y, 1.0)
t_std = ridge(standardize(X), y, 1.0)
print("                       raw         standardized")
print(f"theta1 (small scale): {t_raw[1]:9.4f}     {t_std[1]:8.4f}")
print(f"theta2 (large scale): {t_raw[2]:9.6f}     {t_std[2]:8.4f}")
```

## R
```{webr}
# Two features on wildly different scales; the small one carries the signal
x1 <- c(0.011, -0.004, 0.009, -0.013, 0.006, -0.008, 0.015, -0.002,
        0.010, -0.011, 0.003, -0.007, 0.012, -0.005, 0.001)
x2 <- c(820, -540, 410, -930, 360, -610, 1180, -150,
        770, -880, 240, -470, 990, -330, 80)
y  <- 100*x1 + 0.001*x2 + c(0.02, -0.01, 0.015, -0.02, 0.01, -0.012, 0.018,
        -0.003, 0.014, -0.016, 0.005, -0.009, 0.017, -0.006, 0.002)

ridge_fit <- function(X, y, lambda) {
  n <- ncol(X); m <- nrow(X); P <- lambda * m * diag(n); P[1, 1] <- 0
  solve(t(X) %*% X + P, t(X) %*% y)
}

X <- cbind(1, x1, x2)
t_raw <- ridge_fit(X, y, 1.0)
Z <- X
Z[, -1] <- scale(X[, -1], center = colMeans(X[, -1]),
                 scale = apply(X[, -1], 2, function(c) sqrt(mean((c - mean(c))^2))))
t_std <- ridge_fit(Z, y, 1.0)
cat("                       raw         standardized\n")
cat(sprintf("theta1 (small scale): %9.4f     %8.4f\n", t_raw[2], t_std[2]))
cat(sprintf("theta2 (large scale): %9.6f     %8.4f\n", t_raw[3], t_std[3]))
```

:::

Raw, ridge crushes the signal-carrying coefficient to about $0.0002$, though its true value
is $100$. Standardized, the two coefficients are comparable, near $0.52$ and $0.51$.

The one knob left is $\lambda$ itself, chosen by cross-validation against held-out error
rather than by eye (see the model-evaluation page). When predictors are correlated, LASSO
picks one of a group somewhat arbitrarily; [Elastic Net]{.term} adds a ridge term to the L1
penalty to keep correlated features together while still zeroing out the rest; `scikit-learn`
fits it with `ElasticNet`.

::: {.explore}
[Try it]{.lbl}
In the path demo, lower the polynomial `degree` to 4 or raise the comparison `lam0`, and
watch the LASSO nonzero count fall while ridge stubbornly keeps every coefficient. Then drop
the standardization step and see the LASSO path turn to noise: without equal scales, a single
$\lambda$ no longer means the same thing across features.
:::
